Roll an array

Source: R/roll.R
rray-roll.Rd

  • rray_roll() rolls the elements of x along one or more axes, with one roll per axis. Everything along an axis moves by the same amount.

  • rray_roll_each() rolls the elements of x along a single axis, with a separate roll for each row, column, and so on. For example, with a matrix and axis = 2, each row can move by a different amount.

An element pushed off one end circles back on the other.

Usage

rray_roll(x, ..., n, axes)

rray_roll_each(x, ..., n, axis)

Arguments

x

An array.

...

These dots are for future extensions and must be empty.

n

For rray_roll(), an integer vector indicating the amount to roll, either size 1 or the size of axes.

For rray_roll_each(), an integer array indicating the amount to roll for each row, column, etc., as determined by axis. It is broadcast to the dimensions of x with axis set to 1.

axes

An integer vector of axes to roll along.

axis

A single integer representing the axis to roll along.

Value

An array with the same type and dimensions as x.

Details

A positive n moves elements toward the end of the axis, and a negative n moves them toward the start. Rolls circle around, so an n of 7 along an axis with dimension 5 is the same as an n of 2. An n of 0, or any multiple of the dimension, leaves the axis unchanged.

Roll

Rolling an axis with a uniform n can be thought of as a carefully crafted rray_slice(). Along an axis with dimension d, position i of the result comes from position (i - 1 - n) %% d + 1 of x:

x <- c(a = 1L, b = 2L, c = 3L, d = 4L, e = 5L)

n <- 2L
d <- length(x)
i <- seq_len(d)

(i - 1L - n) %% d + 1L
#> [1] 4 5 1 2 3

rray_roll(x, n = n, axes = 1)
#> d e a b c
#> 4 5 1 2 3

rray_slice_axis(x, c(4, 5, 1, 2, 3), axis = 1)
#> d e a b c
#> 4 5 1 2 3

Rolling several axes at once is one rray_slice(), with these locations on each rolled axis and TRUE on the rest.

Since a uniform roll is a slice, names on a rolled axis move with the data, just like they do in rray_slice(). Every other axis keeps its names untouched.

Roll each

rray_roll_each() rolls along a single axis, but each row, column, and so on can move by its own amount. That is why n is an array rather than a vector. It is broadcast to the dimensions of x with axis set to 1, so it holds one n for every row, column, and so on that gets rolled.

Variable rolling can be mimicked with the more flexible indexing of rray_index(). Along axis, the coordinates come from the same (i - 1 - n) %% d + 1 formula as rray_roll(), with a different n for each row, column, and so on. Along every other axis, the coordinates are just the positions themselves.

rray_roll_each() drops names along axis, but keeps all other names. When rows move by different amounts, the output's column 1 can hold data from column c in one row and from column b in another, so the original column names are unlikely to make sense:

x <- matrix(1:6, nrow = 2, dimnames = list(c("r1", "r2"), c("a", "b", "c")))

rray_roll_each(x, n = matrix(c(1, 2), ncol = 1), axis = 2)
#>    [,1] [,2] [,3]
#> r1    5    1    3
#> r2    4    6    2

Because variable rolling can be a bit complicated the first time you see it, we'll work through 2D and 3D examples below.

Two dimensions

Start with a matrix:

x <- matrix(1:12, nrow = 3, byrow = TRUE)

x
#>      [,1] [,2] [,3] [,4]
#> [1,]    1    2    3    4
#> [2,]    5    6    7    8
#> [3,]    9   10   11   12

Rolling along the columns, axis = 2, moves elements within each row. x has dimensions c(3, 4), so n is broadcast to c(3, 1), a one column matrix with one n per row:

n <- matrix(c(1L, 0L, -1L), ncol = 1)

rray_roll_each(x, n = n, axis = 2)
#>      [,1] [,2] [,3] [,4]
#> [1,]    4    1    2    3
#> [2,]    5    6    7    8
#> [3,]   10   11   12    9

The first row moves 1 toward the end, the second row stays put, and the third row moves 1 toward the start.

Rolling along the rows, axis = 1, moves elements within each column. Now n is broadcast to c(1, 4), so it must be a one row matrix:

rray_roll_each(x, n = matrix(c(0L, 1L, 2L, 3L), nrow = 1), axis = 1)
#>      [,1] [,2] [,3] [,4]
#> [1,]    1   10    7    4
#> [2,]    5    2   11    8
#> [3,]    9    6    3   12

The last column has an n of 3 on a dimension of 3, a full circle, so it doesn't move.

Three dimensions

Three dimensions get a bit more complicated, but demonstrate why n must be an array. Think of an array with dimensions c(2, 5, 3) as 3 tables, each with 2 rows and 5 columns:

x <- array(1:30, c(2, 5, 3))

x
#> , , 1
#>
#>      [,1] [,2] [,3] [,4] [,5]
#> [1,]    1    3    5    7    9
#> [2,]    2    4    6    8   10
#>
#> , , 2
#>
#>      [,1] [,2] [,3] [,4] [,5]
#> [1,]   11   13   15   17   19
#> [2,]   12   14   16   18   20
#>
#> , , 3
#>
#>      [,1] [,2] [,3] [,4] [,5]
#> [1,]   21   23   25   27   29
#> [2,]   22   24   26   28   30

Rolling along the columns, axis = 2, moves elements within each row. There are 2 rows on each of 3 tables, so there are 6 separate rows that can each roll by their own n. A vector can't hold one n for each of them, but an array can. n is broadcast to c(2, 1, 3), which is one n for each row on each table:

n <- array(1:6, c(2, 1, 3))

n
#> , , 1
#>
#>      [,1]
#> [1,]    1
#> [2,]    2
#>
#> , , 2
#>
#>      [,1]
#> [1,]    3
#> [2,]    4
#>
#> , , 3
#>
#>      [,1]
#> [1,]    5
#> [2,]    6

rray_roll_each(x, n = n, axis = 2)
#> , , 1
#>
#>      [,1] [,2] [,3] [,4] [,5]
#> [1,]    9    1    3    5    7
#> [2,]    8   10    2    4    6
#>
#> , , 2
#>
#>      [,1] [,2] [,3] [,4] [,5]
#> [1,]   15   17   19   11   13
#> [2,]   14   16   18   20   12
#>
#> , , 3
#>
#>      [,1] [,2] [,3] [,4] [,5]
#> [1,]   21   23   25   27   29
#> [2,]   30   22   24   26   28

Row 1 of table 1 moves 1, row 2 of table 1 moves 2, and so on. Row 1 of table 3 has an n of 5 on a dimension of 5, a full circle, so it doesn't move. Row 2 of table 3 has an n of 6, which circles around to 1.

Broadcasting allows you to provide a smaller n array when either all of the rows or all of the tables roll by the same amount:

# One `n` per row, the same on every table
rray_roll_each(x, n = array(c(1, 2), c(2, 1, 1)), axis = 2)

# One `n` per table, the same for both rows
rray_roll_each(x, n = array(c(0, 1, 2), c(1, 1, 3)), axis = 2)

Examples

# Positive `n` moves elements toward the end
rray_roll(1:5, n = 2, axes = 1)
#> [1] 4 5 1 2 3

# Negative `n` moves them toward the start
rray_roll(1:5, n = -1, axes = 1)
#> [1] 2 3 4 5 1

# Large `n` circles around
rray_roll(1:5, n = 7, axes = 1)
#> [1] 4 5 1 2 3

x <- matrix(1:6, nrow = 2, dimnames = list(c("r1", "r2"), c("a", "b", "c")))

# Roll the columns, names move with the data
rray_roll(x, n = 1, axes = 2)
#>    c a b
#> r1 5 1 3
#> r2 6 2 4

# Roll the rows
rray_roll(x, n = 1, axes = 1)
#>    a b c
#> r2 2 4 6
#> r1 1 3 5

# Roll both axes by the same `n`
rray_roll(x, n = 1, axes = c(1, 2))
#>    c a b
#> r2 6 2 4
#> r1 5 1 3

# Or by one `n` per axis
rray_roll(x, n = c(1, -1), axes = c(1, 2))
#>    b c a
#> r2 4 6 2
#> r1 3 5 1

y <- matrix(1:12, nrow = 3, byrow = TRUE)

# Roll each row by its own `n`, given as a one column matrix
rray_roll_each(y, n = matrix(c(1, 0, -1), ncol = 1), axis = 2)
#>      [,1] [,2] [,3] [,4]
#> [1,]    4    1    2    3
#> [2,]    5    6    7    8
#> [3,]   10   11   12    9

# Roll each column by its own `n`, given as a one row matrix
rray_roll_each(y, n = matrix(c(0, 1, 2, 3), nrow = 1), axis = 1)
#>      [,1] [,2] [,3] [,4]
#> [1,]    1   10    7    4
#> [2,]    5    2   11    8
#> [3,]    9    6    3   12

# Names on `axis` are dropped, since no single name fits each position
rray_roll_each(x, n = matrix(c(1, 2), ncol = 1), axis = 2)
#>    [,1] [,2] [,3]
#> r1    5    1    3
#> r2    4    6    2
